questions.question: Summarize the discussion about setting up the recording equipment
questions.reference_answer: One of the graduate students is working on building the PDA of the future. The idea is to be able to record meetings for personal use and then query them for pertinent information. The data collection will be anonymized to a large extent, but not so much that the meeting does not represent a real scenario. This meeting will be one of the recorded meetings.

oracle.answer: The discussion about setting up the recording equipment included instructions on ensuring wireless mics were on and positioned correctly (about two thumb widths away from the mouth), checking the signal strength on the display, and reading digit strings aloud after signing consent forms. Participants were advised to read digit strings individually rather than simultaneously to avoid cognitive overload. The setup aimed to capture both close-talking and far-field audio for comprehensive data collection.

C asked several questions to that end but clarified that the source of inquiry was curiosity and nothing more. Additionally, C wanted A to explain to the meeting participants what the experiment was for.

questions.question: What did A think about setting up the recording equipment?
questions.reference_answer: A noted that all participants will have to sign a consent form and read out digits and requested that microphones be kept away from the mouth to minimize breathing sounds. A also mentioned that people will be anonymized in the transcript. A explained that the goal was to eventually be able to query meetings for information.

oracle.answer: Based on the meeting excerpts, A thought that setting up the recording equipment was straightforward and provided instructions on how to use the wireless microphone properly. A ensured that participants were aware of how to operate the equipment, such as keeping the microphone about two thumb widths away from their mouths to minimize breath sounds. A also mentioned the importance of the recording setup, explaining that the close-talking microphones would provide high-quality audio for discourse researchers, while the far-field microphones would be used for acoustic research purposes.

questions.question: Summarize the discussion about the experimental setup of the computer navigation system
questions.reference_answer: The computer navigation system will work as follows. The subject of the experiment will familiarize themselves with information about a city. Then, they will be introduced to an advanced navigation system through which they can navigate the city, and they will be given several tasks, like buying stamps. The navigation system will crash, and the subject will be connected to a human operator. Then, the human operator will control the system based on the subject's requests as the subject tries to complete their tasks. Both sides, the assistant and the subject, will be recorded for data collection purposes.

oracle.answer: The experimental setup involves participants familiarizing themselves with Heidelberg's streets from a tourist guide before engaging with a simulated computer navigation system. Participants are given tasks such as finding locations, taking pictures, and obtaining historical information. The system is described as advanced, understanding natural language queries and providing directions. After completing several tasks, the system crashes, transitioning to a human operator who assists with the remaining tasks without knowing the participant's location, simulating a GPS failure. The setup includes a 2D map display showing the participant's progress. The dialogue between participants and the system (either automated or human) is recorded to gather data on user interactions.

questions.question: What did B think about the experimental setup of the computer navigation system?
questions.reference_answer: B explained that the subject of the experiment will first be given texts about a city, so they can familiarize themselves with foreign terms. Then, they will be introduced to a computer navigation system with which they can navigate the city and provided with a set of tasks to complete. Then, the computer system will crash, including the GPS, so the person will not even know where they are, and the human operator will assist them. To find their location, the subject will have to provide visual information to the human operator. B also thought that creating movies of walking would require a lot of technical effort but later claimed that it may be worth it. B clarified that the goal was to see how people communicate in such a scenario.

oracle.answer: B thought the experimental setup of the computer navigation system involved subjects being placed in a simulated environment (either a 3D model or QuickTime animation) of Heidelberg. Subjects had to familiarize themselves with the area by reading a text about Heidelberg, then interact with a supposedly advanced computer system via a phone to complete various tasks such as finding locations, taking pictures, and getting historical information. The system would crash after the third or fourth task, transitioning to a human operator who would assist the subject without knowing their location initially. B also mentioned the possibility of including a map-type display and recorded dialogues between the subjects and the system (both computer and human operator). B seemed supportive of the detailed setup, considering it would yield interesting data.

questions.question: What did D think about the experimental setup of the computer navigation system?
questions.reference_answer: D wanted to know if the videos for the navigation system would be recorded from a first person perspective. D was also trying to understand how ambitious the system was. D learned that the goal was to understand how people reacted and talked in such a scenario. D provided some information about potential candidates for the human operator and wizard roles as well.

oracle.answer: Grad D seemed unsure about the experimental setup of the computer navigation system, particularly questioning its ambition and how interactive it is. Grad D asked whether users need to provide input to the system or if it simply shows them walking through locations like Heidelberg. This indicates that Grad D was trying to understand the scope and interaction requirements of the system.
